rules: Regular election for a full term (2027-2033). Plurality winner; no runoff. Three candidates on the ballot: Chris Pappas (D), John E. Sununu (R), Edmond LaPlante (Constitution). New Hampshire has no early in-person voting; absentee ballots are available only to voters who qualify under state law, and voters can register at the polls on Election Day. Polls close by 8 p.m. Eastern; results are usually reported on election night. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_United_States_Senate_election_in_New_Hampshire ; https://www.sos.nh.gov/2026-election-details

candidates.name: Chris Pappas
candidates.current_or_last_office: U.S. representative for New Hampshire's 1st district (since 2019)
candidates.bio_short: Pappas has represented New Hampshire's 1st congressional district since 2019 and earlier served on the state Executive Council (2013-2019). He is the first openly gay man to represent New Hampshire in Congress.
candidates.primary_result: Won the September 8, 2026 Democratic primary with 65.0% (100,088 votes) over Karishma Manzur (32.7%) and three others.

candidates.name: John E. Sununu
candidates.bio_short: Sununu served in the U.S. House (1997-2003) and the U.S. Senate (2003-2009); he lost reelection in 2008 to Jeanne Shaheen. He is the son of former Gov. John H. Sununu and the brother of former Gov. Chris Sununu.
candidates.primary_result: Won the September 8, 2026 Republican primary with 68.4% (75,839 votes) over former Sen. Scott Brown (26.6%) and six others.

candidates.name: Edmond LaPlante
candidates.current_or_last_office: Member of the Monadnock Regional School Board
candidates.bio_short: LaPlante chairs the Constitution Party of New Hampshire, whose ballot-access petition succeeded in September 2026, per Wikipedia and Ballot Access News. No FEC financial summary was found for him.
candidates.primary_result: Constitution Party nominee (ballot access by petition).

polls_note: Polls with field_end on or after 2026-09-01, taken from the Wikipedia race page polling table (used as an index), with the pollster/sponsor link given there (source_url; often the pollster's or sponsor's own release, sometimes a news report). Multiple rows with the same pollster and dates are different versions of one poll (LV vs RV, full ballot vs two-way, leaners pushed); see notes. partisan_sponsor follows Wikipedia's (R)/(D) tag on the pollster ('none' = untagged, or a bipartisan R+D pollster pair); sponsor text is Wikipedia's footnote. Results are percentages as published; null = not reported. 'Other' may include named minor candidates (see notes, copied from Wikipedia footnotes). No averages or aggregates are included.

events.what: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen announced she would not seek reelection.
Sen. Jeanne Shaheen endorsed Pappas, WMUR reported.
President Trump endorsed Sununu, The Hill reported.
Former Vice President Kamala Harris endorsed Pappas, The Hill reported.
The Constitution Party's ballot-access petition succeeded, putting Edmond LaPlante on the ballot.
Primaries: Pappas won the Democratic primary with 65.0%; Sununu won the Republican primary with 68.4% over Scott Brown.
Pappas and Sununu held their first general-election debate in North Conway, hosted by the Mount Washington Valley Economic Council.

The Boston Globe reported that New Hampshire Public Radio canceled an Oct. 29 forum after Sununu declined to take part, and that Pappas had earlier declined a debate New England College intended to host.

early_vote.summary: New Hampshire does not offer early in-person voting; only absentee ballots for qualifying voters. No official statewide absentee-return figures were collected.

notes_uncertain: WMUR's Granite State Debate between Pappas and Sununu was scheduled for October 28 at 9 p.m. (Boston Globe, Oct. 22); whether and how it took place was not verified.
The Boston Globe (Oct. 22) also mentions an October 14 forum in Salem, cited by the Sununu campaign; not independently verified.
One Wikipedia poll row (Rasmussen, Sept. 8-10) has 13% 'Other' including several independents who did not make the final ballot.
Edmond LaPlante: no FEC financial summary found.
New Hampshire absentee eligibility rules are summarized from standard state law; not re-verified for 2026.
Ages are as of Election Day (2026-11-03), computed from birth dates on the candidates' Wikipedia pages.
